citation.title: Generative Design by Reinforcement Learning: Enhancing the Diversity of Topology Optimization Designs
citation.authors: Seowoo Jang; Soyoung Yoo; Namwoo Kang
citation.venue: arXiv preprint; later published in Computer-Aided Design 153 (2022), 103225

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: The authors report that a neural approximation of conventional wheel topology optimization generates designs in milliseconds rather than the optimizer's roughly ten-minute runtime.
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: The abstract gives only a qualitative speed comparison. The conclusion describes millisecond inference versus an order of 10 minutes, too imprecise for a numeric ratio.
claim.alternatives: Section 3 reports under 1 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce 1080 Ti against a conventional algorithm taking seconds for simple inputs; another conclusion comparison says milliseconds versus an order of 10 minutes.

baseline.classical_method: Conventional iterative topology optimization used to generate wheel-design training data.
baseline.hardware_classical: CPU; model not identified (abstract and Section 3).
baseline.hardware_ml: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti for reported inference (Section 3); Intel i7 and GTX 1080 Ti for search comparison (Section 4).
baseline.problem_size: Automotive wheel design; 639 reference images for TopOpNet/GDNet training and test in Section 4.
baseline.classical_time: Order of 10 min in general (Conclusion); order of seconds for simple inputs (Section 3).
baseline.ml_time: Less than 1 ms for simple inputs (Section 3); order of milliseconds in the Conclusion.
baseline.data_generation_cost: Conventional optimization is used to generate training data; its cost is described as heavy/time-demanding, but no total cost is quantified (Introduction and Section 3).
baseline.quality_metric: Compliance, pixel difference, and design diversity (Sections 3–4).
baseline.quality_gap: Section 3 reports compliance MAPE comparisons; no single gap stated for the speed claim.

R1.evidence: Section 3 evaluates compliance and says TopOpNet resembles the conventional optimizer, but the abstract's speed comparison does not match output quality or state the classical stopping rule.

R2.evidence: Section 3 compares GPU inference with a CPU-intensive conventional algorithm but does not specify the classical hardware or justify the hardware pairing.

R3.evidence: The Introduction says classical TO generates training data and the Conclusion reports inference speed, but no training or data-generation cost or amortization is reported.

R4.evidence: Section 3 compares compliance of predicted and classical designs; volume feasibility and failed-design rates are not reported as rates.

reporting.n_test_cases: 500 reference images for training and 139 for testing in the cross-comparison (Section 4).

notes: The queue title differs from the title on the accessible arXiv v2 and the later journal article. The open preprint was coded; its article-level results include both TopOpNet and the GDNet diversity framework.
